edges: The interglacial lake landscape is the setting of the Neumark-Nord grease site.
Crushing bones and boiling out the grease is the same method as the recorded bone-juice practice, though the sources are unrelated.
Marrow and back-fat are what hunters who choose the fattest animals are after.
Fat burned for light and fish cooked in pots are two other uses of animal and aquatic fat in the same Ice Age world.
The pull of fat-rich aquatic and sea-mammal foods is a thread from the Aleut sea lion to the Jōmon pot.
Gazelle bones broken for grease in the Levant and bones boiled at Neumark-Nord are the same method, found in two regions and two ages.
The gazelle assemblages show in bone what the recorded marrow practice shows in ethnography.
Wild olives at Ohalo II and heaped oleaster stones across the Mediterranean are two finds of gathered olives.
Marine food at Pinnacle Point and in the Jōmon pots are the oldest and a younger case of sea foods in the human diet.
Nile fish and Jōmon aquatic foods are two Ice Age fisheries.
Xianrendong’s soot-marked pots are the older pottery; the Jōmon pots are those whose contents the lipids reveal.
Shoda finds the Amur’s lower-river pots used for aquatic oils exactly as Craig found for Jōmon Japan.
The San’s craving for animal fat and the explorers’ craving for grease are the same observation from two sides.
Speth’s case that lean meat cannot sustain people is the reason hunters pick the fattest animals.
The Kalahari San’s fats and Pinnacle Point’s marine food are the two African entries of the folio, a hundred thousand years apart.
Hunters who prized the fattest animals and gatherers who tended avocado groves were after the same energy-dense food.
Speth’s explorers craved grease; the insect eaters of the tropics found it in grubs and termites.
The Kalahari San’s mongongo nuts and eland fat sit beside the insect fats of the tropical forest and Australian rock shelters.
